title: Benchmarks with RTX 3080
summary: What a 10 GB RTX 3080 can and cannot do for machine learning, from first principles. Specs, honest measurement, and ceilings you can check any benchmark against.

posts.title: The card on paper
posts.summary: Every spec on the RTX 3080 box reduces to two numbers that decide most ML workloads.

posts.title: Measuring honestly
posts.summary: GPU work is asynchronous, clocks move, and cards throttle. A small timing harness and a short checklist keep the numbers trustworthy.

posts.title: Two ceilings, measured
posts.summary: A copy kernel finds the memory bandwidth ceiling and a big matrix multiply finds the compute ceiling. Compare both to the datasheet.

posts.title: Will it fit in 10 GB?
posts.summary: Model memory is arithmetic. Weights, KV cache and training state, worked out in bytes before you download anything.

posts.title: Tokens per second is a bandwidth problem
posts.summary: Generating text one token at a time reads the whole model from memory for every token. That gives a ceiling you can compute before running anything.

posts.title: Choosing an engine for one 10 GB card
posts.summary: Seven months, three setups, one GPU shared by everything. How I went from vLLM to Ollama, with the VRAM budget at every step.

posts.title: A harness, then the sweep
posts.summary: Three small scripts, 15 planned configurations and one question from last time answered with numbers. Raw speed on the 3080, and what it does to the ceilings from posts 1 to 5.

posts.title: Does a bigger model pay off?
posts.summary: Speed is not the question that matters. I ran my agent's decision suite on Qwen3 8B and on a 35B mixture-of-experts model, then put every number from the series in one place.

title: WTF is AI?
summary: A plain-English tour of what "AI" actually means, from machine learning to language models to agents, with no hype and no maths you cannot do on a napkin.

posts.title: AI is a label, not a thing
posts.summary: AI" covers a stack of ideas from rule-based programs to language models. Knowing which layer someone means clears up most of the confusion.

posts.title: Machine learning is fitting a curve
posts.summary: Instead of writing rules, you show a program examples and let it find the rules. Training, inference and overfitting in one small example.

posts.title: Neural networks are lots of tiny dials
posts.summary: A neuron is a weighted sum plus a bend. Stack millions of them and you have a network, and a reason GPUs matter.

posts.title: Language models are autocomplete at scale
posts.summary: Predict the next token, over and over. How that one trick produces fluent text, why it also produces confident nonsense, and what the knobs do.

posts.title: Agents are language models with hands
posts.summary: Give a model tools and a loop and it can act. How agents work, what MCP standardizes, and why access control suddenly matters.
